title: Kaun Hai?
description: A late-night repair job, an impossible complaint, and an old temple-office terminal that refuses to close the ticket.

nodes.text:
At 2:13 a.m., the monsoon cuts power to the temple trust's administrative office. You were sent to repair its obsolete donation-and-complaint terminal before the morning accounts inspection. The dead UPS clicks once and switches itself on.

Beside it: cold tea, damp receipt paper, and a chair whose cushion is slowly rising as if someone has just stood up. The printer feeds a slip marked COMPLAINT 108/1998 — RESOLVED. A brass service bell rings inside the locked records corridor. A crow taps the window: one, pause, eight.

The terminal asks, "Kaun hai wahan?"

The complaint was filed on 17 August 1998 by Kamla Joshi, accounts assistant. She wrote that night clerk Devendra Sahu had not abandoned his post. He had found donation receipts entered twice after a flood-relief collection and asked for an inquiry.

The resolution says EMPLOYEE LEFT WITHOUT NOTICE. The inquiry field is blank. Kamla's signature appears beneath it, too neat to belong to a carbon copy.

The printer adds a wet line in red: RESOLVED BY WHOM?

The carbon-copy register occupies a steel cupboard labelled CURRENT, which is optimistic by twenty-eight years. Page 108 has been torn out. Pressure marks remain on the sheet below: a date, the word "corridor," and three initials pressed hard enough to score the desk.

Red account thread stitches a cardboard tab over the missing page. Someone wrote CHECK PRESSURE COPY on it. Monsoon water noses under the office door, then stops short of the cupboard.

The side of a drawer pencil brings up the old pressure marks.

"Closure dictated by J.N.B. Original receipt sheet retained in corridor room. Devendra refused revised entry. Kamla did not sign."

Below that, in another hand: "If this page is removed, the complaint remains open. Status is not an investigation."

The initials match no name on the current staff board. The terminal's UPS relay clicks twice, impatient with your reading speed.

choices.label: Take the register to the terminal

nodes.text:
Your query returns three lines:

CLOSING OFFICER: ADMINISTRATOR
ACCOUNT: NOT FOUND
AUTHORITY: CONTINUING

The cursor drops to a field labelled NIGHT CLERK NAME. Behind you, the recently occupied chair gives a small wooden complaint. The terminal does not repeat its question. It waits with the confidence of an office form that knows somebody, eventually, will fill the wrong box.

The terminal accepts your name and quietly changes the date to 18 August 1998. ROLE is already filled: NIGHT CLERK.

A note taped beneath the keyboard says, "If complaint 108 wakes, sign the night-clerk field. Do not answer the fourth bell. — S. Rao."

The laminated staff roster lists S. Rao's service as ended in 2003. Someone later added, in careful blue ink, "died during night duty." The chair behind you settles another centimetre.

The crow is soaked but composed. It taps one beat, then none, then eight. When you lean closer, it repeats the pattern against a pane painted shut before you were born.

On the sill inside lies a curl of damp receipt paper. Each tap makes the printer advance by exactly one line. The paper has wrapped itself around the cold tea glass, preserving a message on its dry inner face.

The rhythm is 1-0-8, not a bird asking to be let in. Unrolling the receipt paper reveals S. Rao's handwriting: "The system only needs a responsible night clerk. Give it a name and the ticket sleeps. Never open the corridor after three bells."

A second sentence has bled through from the reverse: "Rao followed this procedure. Rao never went home."

Outside, the crow waits for you to notice the contradiction.

choices.label: Doubt the note and check the corridor

nodes.text:
The records corridor is locked with a chain on the office side. This should make it reassuring. It does not.

A brass service bell hangs beside the frame, the kind once used to call the night clerk from the ledger room. It is not part of the shrine. Its cord disappears through the wall toward the old records room.

Monsoon water gathers at the threshold without crossing it. From beyond the door comes the scrape of a chair being drawn up to a desk.

choices.label: Read the note on the frame
Ask the terminal for the key

nodes.text:
Two instructions share the doorframe.

The older one, pencilled beneath the paint, reads: "Three calls bring a witness. The fourth enters the statement."

A newer notice, stamped by ADMINISTRATION, covers half of it: "After the third bell, do not open. Enter the current clerk's name and mark resolved."

The newer notice carries J.N.B. in the approval box. Its ink has not faded. A loose wooden panel sits below the bell cord.

The first ring is ordinary brass. The second comes back from farther down the corridor. At the third, the chain drops without being touched.

In the office, the printer writes WITNESS PRESENT. The crow stops tapping. The corridor door opens a finger's width, releasing the smell of wet paper and the precise click of a UPS relay from 1998.

The bell cord remains in your hand. The pencilled instruction promised that a fourth ring would enter the statement. It never said whose.

The latch is free. Inside, donation ledgers sit above the flood line on brick supports. The original sheet for complaint 108 is pinned beneath an administrator's rubber stamp.

Devendra's note says the relief receipts were backdated and entered twice. He refused to replace the originals. Kamla requested an inquiry after he vanished during the next night shift. Her request was closed with a copied signature.

Nothing here accuses the temple or its worshippers. The theft belonged to an office, and the office had filed itself as innocent.

The terminal assembles its audit trail beside the surviving paper record. Devendra reported altered donation receipts. Kamla demanded an inquiry. The closing note was dictated under the initials J.N.B.; her signature was copied; no investigator was assigned.

A final field appears:

REASON FOR REOPENING:

The cursor waits. Somewhere beyond the corridor, a man turns one page of a ledger and stops.

choices.label: Put your name in the Night Clerk field

nodes.text:
The terminal places the complaint scan beside its audit log. The resolution was entered at 2:13 a.m., eleven minutes after Devendra's last receipt correction. Kamla's staff account was not used. An administrator command supplied a picture of her signature taken from a salary acknowledgement.

The initials J.N.B. appear only in the paper impression. They are evidence of an instruction, not proof of who typed it. The terminal asks which claim the records can support.

The timestamps settle into an ugly sequence: corrected receipts, Devendra's objection, Kamla's inquiry, copied signature, closure. No investigation appears between them.

On paper, the copied signature is almost perfect. It repeats a broken loop in Kamla's name that appears on the salary form but nowhere in her handwritten complaint. The printer produces both samples on one damp strip and leaves a box for your finding.

The terminal accepts the finding, then asks a narrower question:

DID YOU WITNESS THE EVENTS OF 18 AUGUST 1998?

The chair waits behind you. The corridor offers no helpful sound. You did not see Devendra object or Kamla file her complaint. You have seen the original paper, the copied signature, and the audit trail tonight.

The distinction feels small enough for an office to ignore and large enough for the dead to keep.

choices.label: State only what the records prove

nodes.text:
The red word RESOLVED peels away from the screen. In its place: PENDING WITNESS STATEMENT.

The terminal asks whether you personally saw the 1998 events. The honest answer is no. It asks whether the closure record was falsified. The paper and audit trail agree that it was.

Three signature fields open. One says WITNESS TO RECORDS. One says NIGHT CLERK. The last says ADMINISTRATOR OVERRIDE and is already signed UNKNOWN.

choices.label: Sign as witness to the records

nodes.text:
The terminal stamps your name into the NIGHT CLERK field and backdates the appointment to 18 August 1998.

DUTY STATUS: PENDING ARRIVAL

The office telephone rings once. Its cable ends in a bare copper knot under the desk. A fresh cup of tea appears beside the old one, equally cold. The chair is now pulled out for you.

At the bottom of the form, PAY REVISION is marked PENDING. Some administrative traditions survive every management committee.

The maintenance override offers two commands: ERASE COMPLAINT and FORCE RESOLUTION. Both require administrator authority.

Before you touch the keyboard, the authority field fills itself: UNKNOWN. The terminal is not asking you to become administrator. It is asking you to confirm that somebody already is.

The UPS relay begins clicking in the crow's 1-0-8 rhythm. The locked office door unlatches, but the corridor door opens wider.

choices.label: Cancel and enter a witness statement

nodes.text:
You state only what the surviving records prove: the closure was falsified, Kamla's signature was copied, and Devendra's report was never investigated.

The terminal prints a dry receipt.

COMPLAINT 108/1998
STATUS: CLOSED AFTER INQUIRY ORDERED

The brass bell rings once. The chair behind you is empty and plainly old. At dawn, the inspector finds the original sheet waiting on the desk. She reads it twice, then asks for the current trustees and a fresh register.

The UPS switches off. This time, it stays off.

You accept. The office clock keeps 2:13 and the rain holds its place on the window.

The terminal closes complaint 108 under RESPONSIBLE CLERK APPOINTED. It opens complaint 109. Then 110. The chair fits better after the third file.

At nine in the morning, the inspector asks the trust secretary why the repair technician never arrived. Inside the locked office, your attendance sheet marks you present for a night shift that began in 1998.

The salary column remains pending.

You confirm the override. Complaint 108 closes at once. So do every open complaint on the terminal, including tomorrow's.

LOGIN ACCEPTED: ADMINISTRATOR UNKNOWN

The keyboard stops responding to you. Forms continue opening, approving themselves with Kamla's copied signature. The printer produces a staff card bearing your photograph, no name, and an authorization level higher than the trust has ever issued.

Behind you, the corridor chair turns to face the office. No one is sitting in it.

You ring the fourth bell.

The office answers from 1998. Rain climbs from the floor to the ceiling. The terminal prints Kamla's missing complaint in your handwriting, including a final sentence you have not yet written: "The witness entered willingly."

The corridor door opens onto the same office, with newer paint and older calendars. At both desks, the chairs are occupied just beyond the angle of sight.

Outside the window, the crow taps once and waits for the zero.
